2026-11-02.patch_summary: This patch breaks out the gup_fill_pages() helper from the __get_user_pages() function, allowing it to be reused by other functions in the follow_page_mask() call chain. The helper fills pages[] and flushes each page's caches in a loop. No functional changes are intended with this patch. It is a refactoring effort to improve code organization and reusability.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David questioned the necessity of checking if pages exist before filling them, suggesting it's unnecessary and potentially error-prone.

Reviewer David pointed out that the gup_fill_pages() function uses a loop variable 'subpage' which is misleading, as it's not actually accessing sub-pages but rather incrementing the 'page' pointer.

Reviewer David suggested that the patch could be based on the gup-fast batching series, which might not require the magic of flushing caches and dcache pages in an open-coded loop.
reviews.raw_body:
Why is that check needed? Why should someone try filling something that doesn't
exist?

---

There is no such thing as a subpage as Willy keeps saying :)

Why not reuse "page" ?

	for (i = 0; i < nr; i++, page++) {

---

Now I wonder why GUP-fast doesn't need any of that. Likely because architectures
that support GUP-fast don't need any such magic.

Maybe we should in fact base this on the gup-fast batching series and also use
the helper in there (passing vma=NULL)?

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that faultin_page_range() and populate_vma_page_range() both call the GUP code with a NULL pages pointer, but did not indicate whether this is an issue or how it will be addressed.

Author Rik Riel addressed David's concern about cache flushes in GUP-fast by explaining that most callers already handle VIVT cache aliasing, and proposed two possible solutions to the asymmetry: adding dcache flushing to unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() or moving it to the GUP callers. No fix is planned for this patch.

Author responded to David's feedback by asking for clarification on which GUP-fast batching series is being referred to and whether both paths should use the same gup_fill_pages() helper, indicating no immediate plan to address a specific technical issue.
reviews.raw_body:
faultin_page_range() and populate_vma_page_range
both call the GUP code with a NULL pages pointer.

---

These cache flushes seem to be common on architectures
with virtually indexed caches, where the cache needs 
to be flushed if the memory is accessed through a 
different virtual address than where userspace might
have written data.

On 32 bit ARM, MIPS, and sh, the kernel seems to
implement an actual cache flush here, but also
claims to support GUP-fast.

I don't understand how that would possibly be safe,
since the pages returned by GUP-fast could be
accessed under a different cache alias than where
userspace accesses the memory.

I think one reason GUP-fast can get away without
a dcache flush is that most of the callers take
care of that, for example by using raw_copy_to_user()
to copy data using the user's virtual address, which
takes care of VIVT cache aliasing.

Likewise, drivers that do zero-copy DMA into user
memory will get the cache flushed on VIVT architectures
inside dma_unmap().

The dcache flush inside GUP covers rarer cases, where
the kernel accesses memory at a different address than
where userspace wrote to that memory.

 cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline              KERNEL
 ----                                 -------------------
 read(buf=U)
   -------------------------------->
                                      get_mm_cmdline(mm, U):
                                        access_remote_vm(mm, arg_start,
                                          kbuf, len, FOLL_ANON):
                                          get_user_page_vma_remote()
                                          (slow GUP + its flushes)
                                          kmap_local_folio(P)
                                          memcpy(kbuf <- K)   // read
                                          kunmap_local(K)
                                        copy_to_user(U, kbuf) // write
                                          through U itself
 read buf at U
   ------>
            clean: the final write to U went
            through U. Same line. No hazard.

In this case, the dcache flush in slow GUP ensures
that data written before the GUP is visible to the
reader.

In the write path, e.g. for PTRACE_POKE, __access_remote_vm
flushes after the write has been done, so the other
process will see the data on the next read.

It looks like process_vm_writev() might be missing that
cache flush after a write, though.

However, now we have a situation where:
1) Only a few oddball callers of GUP need the dcache flush, and
2) Those need to do their OWN flush after a write, and
3) The dcache flush is not needed for most other GUP callers.

We could do two different things here to solve the
asymmetry.

Either we could add dcache flushing to 
unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock(), and make sure all
the callers that need to call that function, or
we could move the cache flushing to the GUP callers.

Then we have KSM, which uses GUP, and which would like
to see the latest page contents...

---

I just moved this code out of __get_user_pages(),
but if we can get rid of it completely by using
a different helper, all the better.

Which GUP-fast batching series are you talking
about, here?

In Yeoreum Yun's series, the batch filling seems 
to be done inline in gup_fast_pte_range(), and not
in a helper:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261102-refactor_gup_fast-v2-4-bc1ac018c834@arm.com/

Should both paths be using the same gup_fill_pages()
helper?

The cache flushing part is broken out into its own
helper function later in this series, so we could
sequence those differently.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary:
reviewer pointed out that the patch's check for a non-existent pages array was unnecessary, as it was already absent in the original code

Reviewer David noted that the patch is inconsistent, undocumented, and error-prone, specifically questioning whether GUP-fast should also flush the dcache for consistency and requesting clarification on when to call this function

Reviewer David suggested breaking out a separate helper function for filling pages, similar to what was done in gup_fast_pmd_leaf, and proposed distinguishing between gup and gup-fast using the VMA argument.
reviews.raw_body:
That's not what I meant. I know that we have GUP users without
pages array.

In the code change you are performing the check is not required.

That's why there wasn't one in the first place.

---

It's all very inconsistent. And undocumented. And error prone.

Could we have GUP-fast also flush the dcache for consistency or
must that only be called with the PT lock held?

---

We also have gup_fast_pmd_leaf that fills an array. I think all of these should
just use a helper (instead of manually looping).

For now we can distinguish gup vs. gup-fast using the VMA argument.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author is considering adding a check to gup_fill_pages() to ensure pages exist before attempting to access them, rather than relying on callers to perform this check.

The author is addressing David's concern that gup_fast callers may need dcache flushes, explaining that most callers either perform DMA operations or access pages through user virtual addresses, and suggesting moving cache flushes to __get_user_pages() instead.

Author agrees that other parts of the code could benefit from the same gup_fill_pages() helper function, and plans to apply it in a future version (v2)
reviews.raw_body:
It looks like 2 of the 3 callers of gup_fill_pages()
check for pages existing. The other does not.

Should we just have the check in this one place, and
not depend on the caller?

---

I think we could, but it does not look like any of
them need it.

Out of the 83 callers of gup_fast, many DMA into the
page, and the drivers do their own flushing. Also,
flushing before the DMA write doesn't help.

KVM, Infiniband, and others pin the pages, sometimes
for longer periods of time, and either flush around 
their reads and writes, or run only on architectures
where we don't need to.

The others access the page through the user's own
virtual address, which again does not require a
dcache flush.

Only a small number of slow GUP callers need dcache
flushes.

It may make more sense to move the cache flushes
all the way out into __get_user_pages() and away
from the follow_page_mask() call chain, so we can
maybe merge more of the helper functions between
slow GUP and fast GUP.

---

I think all of those could use the same helper
function I am breaking out here, once the dcache
flushing moves to its own helper.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) noted that the patch description should explicitly state what functional changes are intended and expressed skepticism about the usefulness of breaking out gup_fill_pages() helper, but acknowledged it could make calling code nicer.
reviews.raw_body:
That should be spelled out in the patch description.

The change as it stands in this patch looks useless :)

Although trying to fill something that doesn't exist is a bit weird.

But if it makes the calling code nicer, sure.

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that the patch by itself isn't super useful but agreed to restructure it in a future version (v2) to split out array filling from cache flushing, allowing for shared helpers between GUP-fast and regular GUP.

Author is addressing David's concern about the scope of changes by suggesting a way to limit the impact of breaking out gup_fill_pages() helper, proposing either folding in additional callers or sending them as a separate series.
reviews.raw_body:
I agree this patch by itself isn't super useful.

It's goal is to be able to have this code in one
spot, and not in multiple places in gup.c

I'll split out the array filling from the cache
flushing, so we can move the cache flushing out
from under the lock, and have GUP-fast and regular
GUP share the same helper.

---

It really doesn't look too bad. Here are all
the GUP callers that need a cache flush:
- kernel/events/uprobes.c (through get_user_pages_remote)
- /proc/pid/cmdline (through access_remote_vm)
- fs/proc/base.c (through access_remote_vm)
- kernel/trace/trace_events_user.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- arch/x86/kernel/cpu/sgx/ioctl.c (get_user_pages ... urgh)
- kernel/ptrace.c (access_remote_vm)
- mm/process_vm_access.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- fs/exec.c (pin_user_pages_remote)
- virt/kvm/async_pf.c (get_user_pages_remote)

In other words, if we change the SGX code to just
call get_user_pages_remote(), and then move the
cache flushing to get_user_pages_remote() and
pin_user_pages_remote() we should be all set.

Want me to fold that into this series, or send
it in as a small, separate prequel series?

As a separate series it would:
1) split out the gup_fill_pages() and gup_flush_pages()
   helpers
2) convert the SGX code to use get_user_pages_remote()
3) move the flush call up the stack into pin_user_pages_remote()
   and get_user_pages_remote()

Just let me know if you prefer that separate, or
folded in. 

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

2026-11-03.patch_summary: This patch breaks out the gup_fill_pages() helper from the __get_user_pages() function, allowing it to be reused by other functions in the follow_page_mask() call chain. The new helper fills pages[] and flushes each page's caches in a separate loop, reducing code duplication and improving maintainability. No functional changes are intended with this patch, which is part of an 8-part series of patches.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer David suggested breaking down the patch into two steps: first, move the existing code to a helper function (gup_fill_pages), and then consider adding batching for gup-fast paths in a future step.
reviews.raw_body:
That sounds like the right cleanup.

Likely you can defer 1) and just do 2) + 3) first.

1) then on top of the gup-fast batching if possible.

-- 
Cheers,

David
